meta.topic: Hundreds of similar complaints within 20 minutes

problem:
Meridian Bank runs a retail mobile banking service used by several hundred thousand customers. On a weekday morning, between 09:12 and 09:32, the contact centre receives more than 300 complaints with the same shape: customers report a debit that does not match the payment status shown in the app, or a credit they expected that has not appeared. Social media posts repeat the same wording, and branch staff report customers arriving in person with the same concern. The technical cause is not yet known, and the incident bridge has only just been opened.

The operations team does not yet know how many customers are affected, how much money is involved, or whether the problem is still happening. Some complaints may describe the same underlying payment twice, once from the payer and once from the payee, so a raw complaint count is not an affected population. A second batch file is due to be processed within the hour, and nobody can yet say whether it is safe to release it. Every minute of delay increases customer harm and the risk that a well meant fix, such as a bulk re-credit, creates duplicate compensation.

The bank must bound the financial exposure, identify the common failure window, stop further harm, and preserve evidence, all before the root cause is known. The case is about sequencing: containment and quantification first, root cause analysis in parallel, and remediation only under maker-checker control once the affected set is proven.
solution:
Start with an incident bridge that separates three workstreams: customer and financial containment, technical root cause analysis, and communications. Containment owns the affected-transaction register, the decision on the next batch, and any remediation. Root cause owns logs, queue state and downstream confirmations. Communications owns one consistent customer message, updated as facts are confirmed, and never states a cause that is not yet proven.

Quantify the population from systems, not from complaint counts. Pull all transactions in the failure window, join them by payment reference and correlation ID across the channel, payment engine, ledger and clearing records, and classify each item as confirmed affected, possibly affected, or unaffected. Value the exposure as the sum of confirmed debits without a matching credit or settlement confirmation, and track it as a single controlled figure that only moves when evidence changes. Hold the next batch until the window is understood, or release only items proven to be outside the affected population.

Preserve evidence before any fix is applied: freeze log rotation for the window, snapshot queue depths and retry state, and record every status change with timestamps. Reconcile the ledger against external payment records item by item. Remediate only from the register, with maker-checker approval, one adjustment per affected payment, and a duplicate check against any later settlement. Close the incident only when the register is empty or fully explained, reconciliation balances, and the root cause has a preventive fix with a named owner.

decision.question: It is 09:35. More than 300 similar complaints have arrived in 20 minutes, the cause is unknown, and a second payment batch is due within the hour. As the duty payments manager, what do you do first?

options.label: A
options.detail: Open a deep technical investigation into the payment engine logs and wait for the root cause before taking any customer or processing action.

options.label: B
options.detail: Freeze the next batch, quantify the affected population and value for the 09:12 to 09:32 window, preserve transaction evidence, and open an affected-transaction register before any remediation.

options.label: C
options.detail: Immediately re-credit every complaining customer in full so complaints stop, then reconcile afterwards.

options.label: D
options.detail: Tell the contact centre the issue is a display error and ask customers to wait 24 hours while engineering investigates.

decisionRationale: B is correct because containment and quantification bound the harm: freezing the next batch stops new exposure, the windowed population count separates real impact from duplicate complaints, and the register makes any later remediation auditable. A is wrong because root cause work can run in parallel but must not delay containment. C is wrong because re-crediting on complaint alone risks duplicate compensation where the original payment later settles. D is wrong because the bank does not yet know it is only a display error, and telling customers that without evidence misleads them.

steps.title: Reports a debit that does not match the app status, or a missing expected credit
Opens the incident bridge and separates containment, root cause and communications workstreams
Extracts all transactions in the 09:12 to 09:32 window and joins them by payment reference and correlation ID
Classifies each item as confirmed affected, possibly affected or unaffected and values the exposure
Freezes the next batch release until the affected population is proven
Preserves logs, queue state and retry state for the window and runs root cause analysis in parallel
Reconciles ledger postings against clearing and scheme status records item by item
Applies approved remediation from the register with maker-checker control and duplicate checks
Issues a consistent customer update based only on confirmed facts and the remediation plan
steps.note: Contact centre scripts and app messaging

steps.title: Closes the incident only when the register is fully explained, reconciliation balances and a preventive fix is owned

happy: The bridge opens within minutes. The windowed extract identifies 412 affected payments worth a single controlled exposure figure, with duplicate complaints de-duplicated by reference. The next batch is held, then released for items proven outside the window. Ledger and clearing records reconcile, remediation is applied once per affected payment under maker-checker control, customers receive one accurate update, and the root cause fix is tracked to closure.

negative.title: Unknown in-flight state
negative.detail: Some payments were accepted by the engine but no downstream confirmation arrived, so their settlement state is unknown. Hold each item in a pending or unknown state, query by correlation ID, and do not retry or reverse it until the downstream status is confirmed.

negative.title: Delayed external confirmation
negative.detail: Clearing or scheme confirmations arrive late, so early reconciliation shows false mismatches. Age the items in the register, re-run reconciliation on a defined cadence, and do not treat a missing confirmation as a failure until the agreed timeout passes.

negative.title: Multiple rails affected
negative.detail: The same window touches more than one rail, each with its own status model and cut-off. Segment the register by rail, apply each rail's status and cut-off rules separately, and never merge rail outcomes into one assumed state.

negative.title: Partial batch impact
negative.detail: Only some items in a batch are affected, and the rest are healthy. Apply item-level outcomes, release healthy items only after proof, and keep accepted items out of any resubmission when rejected items are repaired.

negative.title: Duplicate compensation risk
negative.detail: A customer is re-credited and the original payment then settles, paying them twice. Check every remediation against later settlement and ledger postings, use the register as the single source of remediation, and reverse duplicate credits under the same maker-checker control.

technical: Use the payment reference and correlation ID as the join keys across channel, engine, ledger and clearing records, with event versioning so an older status event cannot regress a newer state. Persist an incident snapshot of queue depth, retry counts and in-flight items at bridge opening. Keep the affected-transaction register as a durable store with state transitions, timestamps, evidence links and maker-checker records, and never edit history in place. Apply idempotency keys to every remediation adjustment so a retry cannot double-post. Retain logs for the window under a hold, and record every status change in an audit trail that shows who decided, on what evidence, and when.

accounting: Debits without a matching credit or settlement confirmation sit as an exposure that must be quantified, not assumed. The ledger is reconciled item by item against clearing records; unmatched items go to a controlled suspense or exception worklist with an owner and an ageing SLA, and are never written off from the register without approval. Remediation postings are separate linked entries that reference the original payment, so the original record stays immutable and the adjustment is traceable. Duplicate compensation is prevented by checking each remediation against later settlement before and after posting. The incident is closed only when the register balances to zero unexplained items and the suspense balance is fully explained.

scenarios.given: customer funds may be impacted and the root cause is unknown
scenarios.then: the team first establishes exposure and prevents further harm. root cause investigation runs in parallel without blocking containment

scenarios.given: a partially valid batch and partial processing enabled
scenarios.then: each transaction receives an independent outcome. only accepted transactions proceed to settlement

questions.question: What should the incident team establish first when customer funds may be affected and the cause is unknown?
options: A press statement blaming a supplier
The affected population, the value exposed, and how to stop further harm
questions.explanation: Containment and quantification bound the harm. Root cause work runs in parallel but must not delay stopping further exposure.

questions.question: Why is a raw complaint count not the affected population?
options: The same payment can be reported twice, by payer and payee, and some complaints may be unrelated
questions.explanation: Complaints must be de-duplicated by payment reference and correlation ID and joined to system records before the affected set is known.

questions.question: What control prevents duplicate compensation during remediation?
options: A single affected-transaction register with maker-checker approval and a duplicate check against later settlement
Asking the customer to promise not to spend the money
questions.explanation: One register, one adjustment per affected payment, and a check against later settlement stops a re-credit plus a late settlement paying twice.

questions.question: When a batch is only partly affected, what is the correct handling?
options: Resubmit the entire batch including accepted items
Apply item-level outcomes, release only items proven healthy, and never resubmit accepted items with repaired ones
questions.explanation: File-level and transaction-level acceptance are separate. Accepted items must not be resubmitted when rejected items are repaired.
